rv.q: Dance-heavy adaptation of Haruki Murakami’s novel is often wildly inventive
It’s an entertaining and audacious endeavour – the book is better, but there’s room for both.
Decouflé's production retains the absurdist tropes but will leave you none the wiser about what Murakami has to say about human consciousness and the struggle to truly know ourselves.

So what a delight to be able to report that Philippe Decouflé’s production is an exquisite dramatisation of the novel, filled with stunningly sculpted stage pictures, haunting music, and elegant choreography.
Visually and choreographically, the production is an absolute triumph.
This adaptation (almost three hours long) drifts when it could punch and delights in its own existence, almost to the exclusion of us on the other side of the fourth wall.
The result is a sensory spectacle that feels perfectly Murakami: dreamlike, dazzling and totally different to anything you’ve seen before.
End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland is a new adaptation of Haruki Murakami’s classic novel, which weaves together two complex stories and very different worlds.
Although there remains considerable scope for the adaptation to develop and explore the novel’s themes more fully, it succeeds in bringing much of Murakami ’s distinctive atmosphere to the stage.

cn.t: Critics praise the visually stunning choreography and immersive spectacle, but find Murakami's complex narrative difficult to translate to stage, resulting in a confusing though dazzling production.
